newsitem.title: UK: Investors switch to UK midcaps as pound tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Investors switch to UK midcaps as pound tumbles.

text.p: British mid-cap stocks were reawakened this week as the FTSE 100 index stalled at historic levels and the pound continued to slip from recent peaks, breathing fresh life into currency-sensitive industrial stocks.

The Mid-250 index, heavily loaded with Britain's biggest manufacturers, has risen four percent in the last four days as the interest rate outlook has dramatically changed, sending sterling rattling back down from its highs.

"The dynamics inside the UK market in the last few days have clearly reflected the view on interest rates and sterling," said Mike Young, European strategist at Goldman Sachs. "It has made the producing side of the economy look more attractive and the manufacturers are disproportionately represented in the midcaps."
On Friday the FTSE 100 index closed down 55.5 points while the Mid-250 index was up almost the same amount, ending up 52.3 at 4,650.5.
Traders and analysts said investors were switching out of leading stocks on the perception that the UK stock market was entering the late cycle of the bull market.

"Fund managers are trying to adjust their portfolios into the manufacturing and export-orientated stocks that predominate in the FTSE 250 index," said Jeremy Batstone, head of research at NatWest Stockbrokers. "These are the stocks that are benefiting from sterling's weakness.

While the leading FTSE 100 index, with a high weighting of financial sector stocks, has risen 25 percent so far this year, the 250 index has languished, rising only four percent and still trading some way off its March peak of 4,729.

The mid-caps 18 percent underperformance against blue-chip stocks so far this year has in part been due to sterling's meteoric rise. Earnings downgrades have dogged Britain's industrial companies and investors flush with cash have sought defensive local earners such as retailers, banks and utilities in the wake of the pound's 17 percent rise against the German market since January.

But after the Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee, when raising official interest rates by a quarter of a point on Thursday, hinted that interest rates may now hold steady at 7.0 percent in the near future, the pressure on Britain's exporters eased.
The pound slid and share prices rallied. Inflation is financial markets' worst fear. Sterling reached a peak of 3.068 marks in July but has fallen four percent in the last three days.

"The strength of sterling has been holding most of the general manufacturing sector down but now people are perceiving rates will be on hold for a while these are seen as the ones to buy," said Batstone. "This is where all the action is."
But conventional wisdom suggests that when the smaller companies join the party, that is the time to get out. In 1987, prior to the stock market crash mid-caps were indeed catching up.

"That was the picture of 1987, the spike in the market was driven by mid-cap companies," said Batstone. "We could conceivably be at a turning point but it's a little premature to start thinking along those lines, volumes are picking up but so far it's just a knee-jerk reaction to sterling."
Goldman's Mike Young points out that the London market is still relatively "cheap" compared with other European markets.
"The liquidity argument is likely to continue to benefit the market as a whole," he said. "Putting it in perspective, the FTSE 100 is still the worst market in Europe."
But strategists warned that sterling's recent fall from grace will not impact on upcoming company earnings which may still suffer from the past effects of the strong pound.

"If sterling has peaked, then expectations for earnings will begin to stabilise and even rise," Young said. "Any adverse reaction to earnings this time around will be seen as an opportunity to take on additional exposure," he added.
Batstone agreed "We must still be extremely careful about picking stocks, but there is no doubt that we're seeing an attempt to re-orientate."
